name: Oruma
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: In terms of the usual typology, dialects 11-12, 312-319 would be classified as two-levei [sic: two-level] tone systems without downstep, dialects 13-311 as two-level tone systems with downstep, and dialects 321-42 as pitch-accent systems. These different characterizations of otherwise closely-related, often mutually intelligible, dialects raise doubts as to the usefulness of this typology. [...] [note 1:] The dialects are here numbered according to a code in which the first digit indicates the language and the later ones indicate subgrouping within the language. The dialect names are abbreviated as follows: OR = Oruma ... BI = Biseni ... OA = Okordia ... [Table 1, row:] 11 OR HH HH HL HH ...

new_statements.rule_in_words: Oruma (Williamson's dialect 11, Inland Ijo cluster) is a two-level (H/L) tone language without downstep; lexical morpheme classes surface in isolation as e.g. Class A HH/HH, Class B HL/HH. As in all Ijo lects, surface pitch is computed over syntactically defined groups whose pattern is determined by the class of the group-initial morpheme ('first morpheme strong, others weak'). Nothing is said about word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Williamson notes that in Table 1 an initial V-syllable sometimes behaves differently from an initial CV-syllable; Williamson & Blench 2006 (ELL2) instead generalise 'inland Ijo' (Biseni, Okordia, Oruma) as 'two tones plus downstep', whereas the 1988 table has Oruma without downstep and Okordia with downstep.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns lexical tone classes of morphemes in isolation (citation forms) and the phonological 'group' (object+verb, noun+modifiers) as the domain of pitch realisation; group-initial morpheme prominence is a phrase-level tonal dominance fact, not word stress. Text was read as verbatim scanned served by archive.org full-text search of the lending scan (scan itself not downloadable); excerpts with provenance saved in the file named.
new_statements.identity_note: Williamson 1988 treats Oruma as dialect '11 OR' of the Inland Ijo cluster (cluster 1: Oruma, Biseni, Okordia) within the Ijo dialect continuum; Williamson & Blench 2006 call it 'Tugbeni (Oruma)', one of three 'isolated languages' of inland Ijo. Same variety as Glottolog orum1241 / ISO orr (Oruma town and Ibelebiri, Ogbia LGA, Bayelsa; an enclave within Ogbia-speaking territory). The ELL2 generalisation ('inland Ijo... two tones plus downstep') covers Biseni (bise1238) and Okordia (okod1238) as well and differs from the 1988 table, which shows Oruma without downstep.

sources.note: Verbatim scanned text obtained via archive.org full-text search of lending scan bwb_P8-AXU-188 (scan not downloadable; excerpts saved). Oruma = dialect 11 'OR' in her 28-dialect Table 1 (p.254; isolation patterns Class A HH/HH, Class B HL/HH); p.253: 'dialects 11-12... would be classified as two-level tone systems without downstep'. Sec. 1.2: in all Ijo dialects pitch is organised over syntactic GROUPS whose pattern is set by the initial morpheme ('first morpheme is strong and the others weak'). No word-stress statement.
